title: Oahu Aerial
summary: A feature rather than a usual Note: a collage of Christian's favorite drone footage from his years living on Oahu, from the Mokes and Lanikai on the east side to manta rays off the North Shore, with a little about the island.

For the "little about Oahu" section, what would you like it to say? I didn't add any facts about the island that weren't in your notes.
Personal: I have lived on Oahu for over 20 years. Not all at the same time but in the 70's and 80's as a kid. After high school and then when I met Helena we moved there together and our kids were born there. They both graduated high school there. We have friends that are as close as family or Ohana there. We visit often. 
Non Personal: Seen from above, Oʻahu is a living contrast of emerald volcanic ridges, turquoise shoals, and open Pacific swells. Hovering across its coastlines reveals how dramatically the island shifts character depending on which heading you fly:

North Shore (The Big Wave Arena): Cruising up the north coast puts raw ocean power directly in frame. Winter swells march in from deep open water, detonating across shallow lava shelves into cavernous barrels at spots like Pipeline, Sunset, and Waimea Bay. From altitude, you catch the sheer scale of the white-water plumes, the curvature of the sandbars, and the tight clusters of spectators lining the golden beaches.

Windward East Side (Reefs & Trade Winds): Bank east past Makapuʻu to reveal vast networks of barrier reefs slicing through vivid neon-turquoise water. The constant offshore trade winds churn up playful surf breaks and kite lines outside Kailua and Waimanalo, while sheltered emerald sandbars and offshore barrier islands like the Mokuluas stand out like stepping stones in the calm shallows.

Leeward West Side (Rugged Sunset Cliffs): Sweeping down the dry Waianae range on the leeward coast offers dramatic, serrated green mountain spines dropping straight toward quiet coves and tide pools. As the afternoon winds drop off into glassy waters, it becomes the premier flight path for tracking open-ocean golden hours and long, trailing shadows stretching out toward Kaʻena Point.

South Shore (Urban Coastline & Sunset Glow): Circling south brings the skyline of Honolulu, the crater bowl of Diamond Head, and the gentle, rolling outer reef breaks of Waikīkī into crisp view. Flying along this coastline at dusk delivers wide-angle panoramas of sun sinking into the Pacific horizon, bathing hotel facades, catamarans, and calm lagoon waters in rich apricot and rose-gold light.

post.title: Oahu from above
post.body:
This one is a different kind of post. There's no ride and no track, just some of the footage I like best from the drone flights I made over Oahu.

Oahu is a big part of my life. I've lived there for over twenty years, though not all at once: as a kid in the '70s and '80s, then again after high school, and later, after I met Helena, we moved there together. Our kids were born there, and they both graduated high school there. We have friends there who are as close as family, our ohana, and we visit often. I was living there when I shot all of these.

I'm FAA certified, and I followed all the rules and regulations on every flight.

I've grouped it loosely by side of the island, because that's how I remember it.

The east side gets most of the frames. Looking down over the Mokes off Kailua and Lanikai. Lanikai Beach at sunrise. Makapuu, where the shorebreak comes in hard and the riders go out into it anyway. A couple of clips of the coast road, following the car along the shore. And one unexpected visitor: a paraglider who just showed up. I hadn't seen them when I took off or while I was flying, and we were very far apart.

On the south shore there's Magic Island.

The North Shore is where the water turns into the subject. Snorkeling around the coves, and then the manta rays: one on its own, a few more, and a pair moving together. From above, they're just shapes gliding under the surface, which is exactly why I kept those clips.

And then there's one that doesn't belong to any side: the kayak and the hammock.

A little about Oahu

Seen from above, Oahu is a contrast of green volcanic ridges, turquoise shallows and open Pacific swell, and it changes character with every side you fly.

The North Shore is the big wave arena. Winter swells come in from deep water and break over shallow reef at spots like Pipeline, Sunset and Waimea Bay. From the air you see the scale of the white water and the curve of the sandbars.

The windward east side is reefs and trade winds. Past Makapuu the water turns bright turquoise over the reef, the trades, blowing onshore most of the time, bring surf and kites outside Kailua and Waimanalo, and the Mokulua islands sit off Lanikai like stepping stones in the shallows.

The leeward west side is dry and rugged. The Waianae range drops toward quiet coves and tide pools, and at golden hour the long shadows stretch out toward Kaena Point.

The south shore is the city coastline: the Honolulu skyline, the crater of Diamond Head and the gentle reef breaks of Waikiki, all glowing at sunset.

The idea for this page is a bit of an experiment. An illustration of the island at the top, with a little drone character flying over it, both made with AI, and the clips laid out below as a collage. Less of a story and more of a postcard.

What I learned: going back through years of footage, the clips I kept weren't the biggest views. They were the ones with something moving in them: a wave, a ray, a car on the coast road.

episode.title: Oahu from above
episode.script:
It started with sunrise over Lanikai, seen from somewhere up in the air.

This one is a little different. There's no trail in it, no climb and no tracker left running in the car. It's a reel of favorites. Christian flew a drone over Oahu across a few years, and when he went back through the footage, these were the clips he kept.

He knows this island. He's lived on it for more than twenty years, just not all at once. First as a kid, in the seventies and eighties. Then again after high school. And later with Ha-Leen-Ah, after they met. Their kids were born there, and both of them graduated high school there. There are friends on Oahu who are as close as family, and they still visit often.

And for the record, Christian is FAA certified, and every one of these flights followed the rules.

***

Most of the clips come from the east side.

There are the Mokes, the two little islands off the coast of Kailua and Lanikai, seen straight down from above. There's Lanikai Beach in the early light. And there's Makapuu, where the shorebreak comes in hard, and the riders go out into it anyway. Christian kept his camera on the water and let them be small in the frame. I'll say this for him: he knows when the wave is the story.

Then there's the drive. Two clips following the car along the shore on the east side. The road, the water, and a car moving between them.

One of the east side clips he calls an unexpected visitor. It was a paraglider. Christian hadn't seen them when he took off, or at any point while he was flying, and the two of them were very far apart. The footage just had a little extra company in it.

***

On the south shore there's Magic Island, seen from the air.

And then the North Shore, where the water itself takes over. There's snorkeling around the coves. And there are the manta rays. One on its own. A few more. And then a pair, moving together under the surface.

From up high, a manta ray isn't much more than a dark shape on blue water. But it's a shape that glides, and Christian held the shot long enough to let it.

***

There's one more clip that doesn't belong to any side of the island. A kayak, and a hammock. That's the whole title, and honestly, it's the whole idea.

***

What strikes me, going through the reel, is what he chose to leave out. Years of flights, and the clips he kept aren't the widest or the most dramatic. Almost every one of them has something moving in it. A wave breaking. A ray turning. A car on the coast road. That's an editor's eye, and it's a harder thing to have than a good drone.

The plan for the page is simple: a little drone up top, and the clips laid out below it like postcards on a table.

***

Some islands you see from the beach. Christian saw this one from a little higher up, and then had the good sense to keep only the parts that moved.
